definition: Bibliomining is the use of a combination of data mining, data warehousing, and bibliometrics for the purpose of analyzing library services.
details: The term was created in 2003 by Scott Nicholson, Assistant Professor, Syracuse University School of Information Studies, in order to distinguish data mining in a library setting from other types of data mining.

explainer.lead: Bibliomining helps libraries learn from the data their services generate. By combining data mining, data warehousing, and bibliometrics, it turns scattered records into evidence that can guide library service decisions.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a librarian trying to solve a puzzle using clues from book checkouts and other library records. Bibliomining means gathering those clues in one place, looking for useful patterns, and using them to improve the library. It is like noticing that many children ask for dinosaur books and deciding to make them easier to find.
tiers.practitioner: In practice, library service data is consolidated in a warehouse, then examined with data-mining and bibliometric methods. The work can support analysis of collections and services rather than general-purpose business reporting. Care is needed when integrating records and interpreting patterns, since a correlation in library usage data does not by itself explain why users behaved that way.
tiers.paperLevel: Bibliomining is formally the combined use of data mining, data warehousing, and bibliometrics to analyze library services. Scott Nicholson, then Assistant Professor at Syracuse University School of Information Studies, created the term in 2003 to distinguish data mining in libraries from data mining in other settings. It names an application area and methodological combination, not a specific algorithm or dataset.

explainer.example: A library warehouses several months of anonymized checkout records and analyzes borrowing patterns by subject and time period. It finds that introductory science books are borrowed heavily at the start of each term, so it schedules a prominent display and reviews whether enough copies are available then.

usedIn.name: Library service analysis
usedIn.detail: Using patterns in library data to examine how services are used.

usedIn.name: Library data warehousing
usedIn.detail: Bringing library records together so they can be analyzed consistently.

usedIn.name: Bibliometric studies
usedIn.detail: Contributing publication-based measures to the broader analysis of library services.

explainer.intuition: Libraries already produce records about their services; bibliomining treats those records as evidence to organize and explore. Its defining idea is to combine several data-analysis approaches specifically for understanding library services.
howItWorks: Gather records generated by library services.
Organize them in a data warehouse for combined analysis.
Apply data-mining methods to identify patterns.
Add bibliometric analysis where publication-related measures are relevant.
Use the findings to evaluate or improve library services.
explainer.whyItMatters: It gives library service analysis a distinct identity and a way to connect stored operational data with systematic pattern discovery. That can make decisions about services more evidence-based than relying on isolated counts or impressions alone.
misconceptions: It is not just another name for all data mining; the term specifically concerns library settings.
It is not a single algorithm, but a combination of data mining, data warehousing, and bibliometrics.
Finding a usage pattern does not automatically establish its cause.
